Docile

DOSS-ul -- two syllables, rhymes with 'fossil'. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Docile is ready to accept control or instruction; submissive.

The rescue dog was surprisingly docile, sitting quietly while the vet examined every paw.

Worked Example

At the petting zoo, the old goat lets toddlers braid its beard, tug its ears, and lead it around by a ribbon without so much as a snort.

An animal that calm and easy to handle is docile. Docile describes a naturally gentle, unresisting temperament -- easily led, easily taught, with no fight to overcome in the first place.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

tractable: Tractable means easily led or managed, and it is all business -- a tractable committee, a tractable problem, anything easy to steer. Docile adds temperament: a docile animal or patient is mild-natured and unresisting by disposition, not merely convenient to manage.

tame: Tame describes an animal that has lost its fear and wildness around humans and will approach people on its own. Docile is about accepting control: a docile creature submits calmly to handling and instruction. A tame raccoon may raid your porch boldly yet be anything but docile when you try to pick it up.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

unruly: hard to control

headstrong: stubbornly determined to have one's own way

Where it sits · how easily it can be managed — gentle → docile → meek

gentle vs. docile: Gentle describes softness of temperament and stops there -- a gentle horse won't hurt you, while a docile one goes further: it accepts the saddle, the lead rope, and the lesson without resistance.

meek vs. docile: Meek goes further than docile: a docile pony accepts the saddle and the lesson, while a meek one would never protest anything at all -- meek is unresisting to the point of never standing up for itself.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — doc-

root — doc-: to teach (Latin docere)

suffix — -ile

suffix — -ile: able to be, easily (Latin -ilis)

Put it together

Put it together: Docile comes from Latin docere, 'to teach,' plus -ile, 'easily able to be' -- literally 'easily taught.' The docile student came first; the docile pony followed: both accept instruction without pushing back.

Use the root in a new word: doctrine

Use the root in a new word: doctrine: The academy's central doctrine was that any student could master mathematics with enough practice.

Root Check

Word Choice

Docile most often describes animals and temperaments: a docile lamb, a docile patient, a docile crowd. It points to a naturally mild, easy-to-manage nature -- the docile one never resists in the first place. When someone actively gives in to another's will, submissive is the sharper word; when they follow rules on principle, compliant fits better.
